newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal urges S.Africa resist Indonesian pressure.
newsitem.headline: Portugal urges S.Africa resist Indonesian pressure.

text.p: Portugal urged South Africa on Tuesday to resist Indonesian pressure after Pretoria expelled the Portuguese ambassador over the leaking of a misdirected letter from President Nelson Mandela to Indonesian President Suharto.

"It is absolutely essential that the arguments of those who want to damage ties between the two countries (Portugal and South Africa) should not prevail," Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Ana Zacarias said, reading from a prepared statement.
"South African authorities should not be susceptible to the poisoning of Portugal by Indonesia," she added.
Portugal said on Monday it deplored the expulsion of its envoy to South Africa over the leaking of the Mandela letter, intended for President Suharto.

Zacarias was speaking after South African ambassador Kingsley Makubela met Secretary-General Francisco Knopfli at the Foreign Ministry to explain the reasons for the expulsion of the Portuguese ambassador last week.

She gave no details of the talks, but said: "Despite our profound disappointment with the disproportionate attitude by the South African authorities, everything will be done on the Portuguese side to ensure that a climate of good relations is maintained between Portugal and South Africa."

Portuguese newspapers on Tuesday quoted foreign ministry sources as saying they believed that South Africa's decision to expel Portuguese Ambassador Vasco Valente was due to pressure from Indonesian authorities.
Mandela had written to Suharto in mid-July, asking him to release East Timorese rebel leader Xanana Gusmao, according to South African sources.
The letter was sent in error to the embassy of Portugal -- the former colonial power in East Timor -- and was neither returned nor forwarded to the Indonesian embassy.
Zacarias said that Ambassador Valente had thought that the letter was a copy for his consideration.

Mandela's proposal was leaked to newspapers in Portugal before Suharto was made aware of it. The incident hurt his attempt to bolster a United Nations effort to resolve the conflict over Indonesia's disputed rule in East Timor.
Zacarias told Reuters earlier that Portugal would not retaliate in kind after South Africa expelled its ambassador.
"We have no intention of asking for the expulsion of the South African ambassador to Lisbon," she said.

South African government sources said the incident had not permanently damaged relations with Indonesia or Portugal, but Valente's was the first diplomatic expulsion by Pretoria since Mandela came to power in historic elections in 1994.
The Portuguese Foreign Ministry on Tuesday urged Mandela to press on with his efforts to settle the dispute over the Pacific territory of East Timor.
"President Mandela should pursue his initiative to obtain the freedom of Xanana Gusmao and other Timorese political prisoners," it said.
In Pretoria at the end of last month, Mandela briefed Portuguese President Jorge Sampaio on his initiative.

Gusmao is serving a 20-year sentence in Jakarta's Cipinang prison for his opposition to Indonesian rule of East Timor. Mandela asked for and received permission to meet him during a state visit to Indonesia in mid-July.
Mandela has since invited Suharto to visit South Africa in November, following a proposed visit by East Timorese bishop and Nobel peace laureate Ximenes Belo in October.

Indonesia invaded East Timor in late 1975, a year after Portugal relinquished colonial rule, and annexed it in 1976. A small group of armed guerrillas is still fighting Indonesian rule, which is not recognised by the United Nations.
